title: AI Can Write the Roadmap. It Can't Run the Room.
author: Empathy Elevated
summary: This piece recaps a Substack Live conversation between the newsletter's host and Aadil Maan, a technical program management writer, on what AI has actually changed about the TPM role. Maan's central argument is that AI has not eliminated the job so much as stripped away the administrative busywork that was obscuring its true function: synthesizing conflicting stakeholder input into a narrative others can act on. He reframes the TPM as organizational 'glue,' arguing that as AI accelerates the volume and pace of inputs (fifty demos replacing one PRD, code shipped in an hour instead of three sprints), the human judgment required to separate real signal from well-formatted hallucination becomes more essential, not less. The piece's sharpest claim is diagnostic: every program failure is fundamentally a people problem, a technology problem, or both, and while AI can accelerate the technology side, it cannot manufacture the psychological safety and cross-functional trust that determine whether people raise problems before they become unfixable. It closes by arguing the coming advantage belongs to generalists with broad pattern recognition across contexts, not narrow specialists, because judging what AI output actually means requires exactly the kind of accumulated organizational discernment a model cannot supply.
points: Maan's reframe of AI's actual effect: it removed the busywork hiding the TPM's real function (cross-stakeholder synthesis) rather than replacing the function itself.
His diagnostic rule that every struggling program is a people problem, a technology problem, or both is offered as a triage tool leaders can apply before reaching for a technical fix.

The claim that AI can accelerate the technology side of an organizational problem but cannot manufacture trust or psychological safety between functions draws a sharp boundary around what AI leadership tools can and cannot fix.

He argues the coming competitive advantage belongs to generalists with broad cross-context pattern recognition rather than narrow specialists, since judging AI output for 'signal vs. well-formatted hallucination' requires exactly that kind of accumulated judgment.
The piece explicitly reframes empathy from a 'soft skill' into organizational infrastructure, arguing it is the capacity that scales when the volume of AI-generated inputs increases.
quotes: AI didn't kill the technical program manager. It just took away the busywork that was hiding the actual job.
Aadil's take was blunt: half of what gets pointed at AI doesn't need AI. It needs someone willing to ask what problem they're actually solving before reaching for a solution.

So when the inputs themselves start changing, when fifty demos replace one PRD, when code that took three sprints now takes an hour, the glue work doesn't disappear. It gets harder to see. And it gets more important, not less, because someone still has to judge what's signal and what's just a well-formatted hallucination.
Every program, he said, is either a people problem or a technology problem, sometimes both. Psychological safety. Trust between functions.

The generalists win in this next stretch, not the specialists who bet everything on one technical lane, but the people who've absorbed enough pattern recognition across companies and contexts to know when something reads well and means nothing.

What it can't do is stand in the room when engineering is exhausted, product is anxious, and finance is asking questions nobody's ready to answer, and hold that space without losing the thread or the people in it. That's still the job. It always was.
